summary:
Same-sex conduct is decriminalised in Belize. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, presided over by Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, struck down the colonial-era Section 53 sodomy law as unconstitutional in the case brought by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco, who filed the challenge in 2010; the hearing was held in Belize City in May 2013, at a time when LGBT activists were receiving violence and death threats. Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn such a statute, and the Human Dignity Trust carries the case among its documentation of constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy laws.

The ruling survived a sustained government appeal. The Government stated on 17 August 2016 that it would not appeal, reversed that position on 9 September after meeting religious leaders, and filed a partial appeal against the declaration that the Constitution bars discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Catholic Church withdrew from the appeal in March 2018, leaving the Government as sole appellant, and Solicitor General Nigel Hawke argued that the judgment amounted to judicial overreach in reading "sex" to include sexual orientation. On 30 December 2019 the Appeals Court upheld the unconstitutionality of Section 53, confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation, and held that freedom of expression includes sexual expression.

Section 5(1)(e) of the Immigration Act still lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Maurice Tomlinson challenged that provision in 2013, was granted leave by the Caribbean Court of Justice in May 2014, and was joined by CARICOM as an interested party in October 2014; the Court dismissed the case on 10 June 2016, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. Belize contended that Section 5(1) applies only to persons offering sexual services for financial gain and is not enforced as a blanket prohibition on homosexual immigrants. The same judgment clarified that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize may bar homosexuals from other CARICOM countries from entering, on account of obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding domestic statutes that prohibit gay entry.

Statutory protection against bias-motivated harm exists alongside the decriminalisation ruling. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly provides prevention and protection from sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity, and Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 makes evidence that an offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance, effective 27 April 2024. In its 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted 15 of 17 recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity, the first CARICOM country to accept that many, pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection; two recommendations on rights equality were noted rather than accepted. The accepted recommendations included educational campaigns to reduce societal stigma, concrete steps to ensure universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people, measures addressing discrimination, violence and hate crimes, and training police officials to respond properly to violence.

No trans-specific rule on identity documents or passport markers appears in the source material at hand, and no youth- or minor-specific care, medication or travel findings are present.
tangentialFactors:
Religious opposition to decriminalisation was organised and public. The Council of Churches held a "Take a Stand" rally on 3 December 2011 and a "Belize Action/Family Forum" rally on 23 November 2011 at which decriminalisation was described as "an orchestrated plan of demonic darkness"; in December 2011 Prime Minister Dean Barrow publicly rejected pressure from President Obama, stating that Belize would not change its laws.

Social attitudes have been polled in ways that cut against an assumption of hostility. A 2013 UNAIDS survey of 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 found 34% accepting and 34% tolerant of homosexuals, among the highest acceptance rates recorded in Caribbean polling. Against that, expat reporting from 2019 argues that the rarely enforced Section 53 had fostered intolerance, citing a 1998 protest against a gay cruise docking as evidence of residual public hostility, while holding that gay travellers have long found Belize friendly.

Belize's position on decriminalisation sits inside regional comparative framing: the Human Dignity Trust treats the Orozco ruling as part of a wider pattern of constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy statutes across the Caribbean, and Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn such a law.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing advocacy infrastructure has expanded since 2016. UNIBAM, the country's organised LGBT advocacy organisation, was the vehicle for the Orozco litigation, and LGBT organisations have become markedly more visible and active since the August 2016 Supreme Court ruling. Belize held its first Pride Week in August 2017, with awareness and acceptance activities hosted throughout the country.

Domestic obligations arising from the Universal Periodic Review process include legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and the collection of SOGI data, alongside educational campaigns to reduce societal stigma and steps to secure universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 and the hate-bias aggravation in the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 operate inside Belize's own criminal and sentencing framework rather than at the border.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced finding on legal gender recognition, gender marker changes on passports or identity cards, or any screening process at entry that could disclose a visitor's trans status; these questions remain unresolved on the material at hand rather than answered in the negative.

Prison practice for transgender detainees is also unresolved. A general reference work on LGBTQ people in prison was retrieved, but its only Belize-specific content is a navigation link in a violence taxonomy: it carries no birth-sex-versus-identity housing rule, no trans-specific unit, and no solitary or segregation practice for Belizean prisoners, so no placement finding can be stated.

No youth- or minor-specific care, medication or travel findings appear in the source inventory. The assessment of traveller-friendliness rests on a single 2019 expat overview rather than on official or monitoring-body documentation, and the 1998 protest it cites is second-hand.
